title: The dative: dem, der, den (Der Dativ)
summary: The third case. After mit, zu, bei, aus, nach, von and seit, der becomes dem and die becomes der. Now am Montag, zum Frühstück and mit Milch finally make sense.
goals: Use the dative after mit, zu, bei, aus, nach, von and seit
Know the dative forms: dem, der, dem, den
Understand the short forms zum, zur, beim, vom, im, am

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 10: Orientation (Wo ist der Bahnhof?, Mit Bus und Bahn)

sections.title: The third case
sections.text:
You know two cases: the subject ([[der Mann]], the nominative) and the object ([[den Mann]], the accusative, Unit 4). The third is the **dative**. Most often it comes after a few small words: [[mit]], [[zu]], [[bei]], [[aus]], [[nach]], [[von]], [[seit]]. After these, always the dative:
- [[mit dem Bus]] ([[der Bus]])
- [[mit der U-Bahn]] ([[die U-Bahn]])
- [[mit dem Fahrrad]] ([[das Fahrrad]])
- [[mit den Kindern]] ([[die Kinder]])

You've used it since Unit 3 without knowing: [[am Montag]] is [[an dem Montag]], [[zum Frühstück]] is [[zu dem Frühstück]], and [[mit Milch]] is a dative too, just without an article to show it.

sections.title: Two things to notice
sections.text:
- Masculine and neuter are the same: [[dem]], [[einem]], [[meinem]]. Feminine is [[der]], [[einer]], [[meiner]]: yes, the same [[der]] as masculine in the nominative.
- In the plural the noun gets an extra -n: [[die Kinder]], [[mit den Kindern]]. Not when it already ends in -n or -s: [[mit den Eltern]], [[mit den Autos]].

sections.title: The seven dative words
sections.text:
- [[mit]] = with; by: [[mit meiner Freundin]], [[mit dem Bus]]
- [[zu]] = to (a person, a place): [[zu meiner Mutter]], [[zum Arzt]]
- [[bei]] = at someone's place, at a company: [[bei meinen Eltern]], [[bei Siemens]] (Unit 1), [[beim Arzt]]
- [[aus]] = from, out of: [[aus der Schweiz]], [[aus dem Büro]]
- [[nach]] = after; to (cities, countries): [[nach dem Kurs]], [[nach Salzburg]], [[nach Hause]]
- [[von]] = from, of: [[von meinem Bruder]], [[vom Bahnhof]]
- [[seit]] = since, for: [[seit Montag]], [[seit einem Jahr]]

Russian needs three cases where German has one: с мамой (instrumental), к маме (dative), у мамы (genitive). German says [[mit meiner Mutter]], [[zu meiner Mutter]], [[bei meiner Mutter]]: always the dative. And German puts the ending mostly on the article; only the dative plural adds -n to the noun.

sections.title: seit + the present
sections.text: [[Ich wohne seit einem Jahr in München.]] = I **have lived** in Munich for a year. English uses 'have lived'; German, like Russian (Я живу в Мюнхене уже год), uses the present tense, because it's still true.

sections.title: The chunks from Units 3-5, explained
sections.text:
- [[am Montag]], [[am Abend]]: [[an dem]]
- [[am dritten Mai]]: [[an dem]], and [[dritten]] gets -en after [[dem]]
- [[im Mai]], [[im Sommer]]: [[in dem]]
- [[in der Nacht]]: [[die Nacht]] becomes [[der Nacht]] in the dative
- [[am See]] (Unit 5): [[an dem See]], a place: Wo? + dative, lesson 2
- [[Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!]] (Unit 3): [[zu dem]]
- [[zum Frühstück]]: [[zu dem]]
- [[mit Milch]], [[mit Karte]]: dative, but no article to show it
- [[zu Hause]], [[nach Hause]]: fixed phrases with an old dative -e

[[Tut mir leid]], [[Es schmeckt mir]] and [[Können Sie mir helfen?]] come in lesson 5.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: I go by bus.
items.explanation: der Bus, and after mit the dative: dem Bus.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap with mein: I live with my parents.
items.explanation: die Eltern (plural), after bei the dative: meinen Eltern.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap with one word (a short form): I'm going to the doctor.

items.question: Which one means 'with my mother'?
items.explanation: die Mutter is feminine: in the dative, meine becomes meiner.
